chapter: Los Angeles scene in the 1930s and 40s
title: Elmer Fain, bandleader turned union agent
summary: Saxophonist Elmer Fain led a band before becoming business agent of Local 767 and later 47.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Yes, indeed, and it's been like that through the years. Well, he was here when I first came here, and guys like -- well, Elmer Fain, who we mentioned earlier. Elmer Fain has been around Los Angeles -- he was here when I first came here, and later I think Elmer Fain might have had an orchestra at that time. I don't remember. But later, Elmer Fain became a business agent for the black union, local 767.
And now he's the business agent for 47.
When I was at Paul Howard's house, his wife brought out some old newspapers and entertainment journals

and there was an article in one of them about Elmer Fajn's group. It had some name -- the Jolly Jesters or something like that. And they'd been in some kind of a dispute with a club owner who hadn't paid them or something. It was a news article.
That was the first time I'd known that Elmer Fajn was a leader.
Yes, he was a leader, and probably that's one of the things that really encouraged him or got him to get into the bit of trying to protect the musicians, you know.
Saxophone. He was a saxophone player, uh-huh.
Because I've only known him since he's been a business agent with the union.
Yes. Well, I've never heard him perform, because ever since I've known him he probably -- he's been into the role of a business agent, you know. Uh-huh.
